Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

5 AUGUST 2019 → 5 AUGUST 2026

SEVEN YEARS SINCE ARTICLE 370:
THE DAY KASHMIR CHANGED DIRECTION
Seven years ago, on 5 August 2019, Jammu and Kashmir underwent the most consequential constitutional reorganisation in its recent history.

The decision was immediately surrounded by anger, apprehension, predictions of permanent instability and declarations that Kashmir would never recover.

Seven years later, the argument must no longer be conducted through slogans.

It must be tested through outcomes.

> What disappeared?
> What emerged?
> What changed on the street?
> What reached the village?
> What entered the economy?
> And what still remains unfinished?

The honest answer is that 5 August was not a magic switch that transformed Kashmir overnight.
It was a structural reset.

It dismantled an exceptional political arrangement that had gradually become the protective vocabulary of dynastic entitlement, institutional ambiguity, separatist mobilisation and permanent emotional blackmail.

For decades, Kashmir was presented as a society that could only be administered through fear, negotiated with through shutdowns and represented through a handful of political families and separatist intermediaries.

The ordinary Kashmiri rarely controlled that narrative.
The gunman claimed to speak for him.
The separatist issued calendars in his name.
The politician traded his sentiment.
The propagandist exported his suffering.
And the shopkeeper, student, labourer and parent paid the bill.

THE STREET HAS CHANGED

In 2018, Jammu and Kashmir recorded 1,328 incidents of organised stone-pelting and 52 organised hartals.

By 2023, both figures had fallen to zero. The same remained true in official data reported through July 2024.

Terrorist-initiated incidents declined from 228 in 2018 to 46 in 2023.

This is not a cosmetic improvement.

It represents the collapse of an entire infrastructure of organised disruption.
There was a time when one WhatsApp message could empty a market.
One separatist calendar could shut an entire district.
One militant funeral could mobilise thousands.
One rumour could interrupt examinations, transport, business and public life.

Kashmir’s economy was being governed not by institutions, but by uncertainty.

Today, the culture of compulsory shutdown has largely disappeared.

The significance is not that Kashmiris have lost their political voice.

The significance is that coercion no longer decides whether a child attends school, whether a shop opens, whether a patient reaches hospital or whether a family can earn its daily income.

That is freedom too.

But honesty also requires a warning:

Terrorism has not vanished.

The Pahalgam attack of April 2025, in which 26 people were killed, demonstrated that Pakistan-backed terrorism retains the ability to inflict pain and disrupt progress.

Therefore, the achievement is not the complete elimination of the threat.

It is the reduction of terrorism’s social command over Kashmir.

The terrorist may still attempt an attack.

But he no longer automatically controls the street after it.

FROM BOYCOTT TO THE BALLOT

For years, elections in Kashmir were conducted under the shadow of boycott calls, threats, selective violence and claims that voting represented betrayal.

In 2024, Jammu and Kashmir voted in its first Assembly election in a decade.

The overall turnout was 63.88%.

The elections were completed peacefully, without major election-related violence and without repolling.

That figure represents more than electoral participation.

It marks a psychological transition.

The same population that was once instructed to remain behind closed doors stepped out to elect its representatives.

The ballot did not resolve every political disagreement.

It did something more important:

It restored the ordinary citizen to the centre of politics.

Democracy replaced the separatist veto.

Political parties were forced to seek votes instead of interpreting silence.

Even parties that opposed the 2019 decision participated fully in the constitutional process created after it.

That is the great irony of post-2019 Kashmir:

Those who continue to describe the new constitutional order as illegitimate now seek authority, office and political relevance through elections held under that very order.

The boycott has ended.

The bargaining has begun.

FROM EXCEPTION TO EQUAL RIGHTS

After the constitutional changes, 170 Central laws that had not previously applied in Jammu and Kashmir were extended to the region.

These included legal protections connected with education, transparency, minority rights, domestic violence, safeguards for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, forest rights and social justice.

For the first time, constitutional protections available elsewhere in India acquired uniform legal application in Jammu and Kashmir.

This did not automatically solve every injustice.

A law written in Delhi has value only when it is implemented honestly in Kupwara, Kishtwar, Poonch, Shopian and Srinagar.

But the principle changed fundamentally:

Rights would no longer depend on whether a regional political establishment considered their application convenient.

Article 370 had been marketed as a shield protecting every Kashmiri.

In practice, it also became a wall behind which several deprived communities remained politically invisible.

Its removal did not erase Kashmiri identity.

It removed the argument that equality before national law was somehow incompatible with that identity.

THE RAILWAY MAP HAS CHANGED

The transformation is now visible in steel, tunnels and bridges.

In June 2025, the 272-kilometre Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link was dedicated to the nation.

Built at an estimated cost of approximately ₹43,780 crore, the project includes:

— 36 tunnels covering around 119 kilometres
— 943 bridges
— The 359-metre-high Chenab Railway Bridge, the world’s highest railway arch bridge
— The Anji Bridge, India’s first cable-stayed railway bridge

Vande Bharat services now connect Jammu and Srinagar, reducing the journey to approximately three hours.

For generations, geography was treated as Kashmir’s permanent disadvantage.

Now engineering is beginning to convert that geography into connectivity.

An apple grower should not have to calculate his future according to a landslide.

A student should not feel nationally distant because a highway is closed.

A patient should not remain isolated by snow.

A business should not lose its market because the mountain has become impassable.

Rail connectivity is not merely infrastructure.

It is economic integration, strategic mobility and psychological proximity.

FROM AIRPORT CONGESTION TO EXPANSION

Srinagar Airport handled around 44.7 lakh passengers during FY 2024–25, despite its existing terminal being designed for a much smaller annual capacity.
In February 2026, a ₹1,677-crore expansion project was approved.
The plan is intended to increase annual passenger-handling capacity from 2.5 million to 10 million and raise peak-hour capacity from approximately 950 to 2,900 passengers.

That tells its own story.

The debate is no longer whether people will come to Kashmir.

The question is whether the infrastructure can accommodate how many are arriving.

TOURISM HAS RETURNED TO SCALE

Jammu and Kashmir recorded approximately 1.78 crore tourist arrivals in 2025, including around 36,000 foreign visitors.

These figures include different categories of visitors and pilgrimage traffic, and tourism remains vulnerable to security incidents.

Nevertheless, the direction is unmistakable.

Hotels that once calculated losses through curfew calendars now calculate occupancy.

Taxi drivers once trapped by shutdowns now depend on the length of the tourist season.

Houseboat owners, guides, artisans, restaurant workers, pony operators and small traders are again connected to a functioning visitor economy.

Earlier, instability was exported as Kashmir’s primary image.

Today, millions arrive to experience Kashmir directly.

That weakens propaganda more effectively than any press conference.

THE ECONOMY IS EXPANDING BUT MUST BECOME MORE INCLUSIVE

Jammu and Kashmir’s nominal economy is estimated at approximately ₹2.86 lakh crore in 2025–26.

Real GSDP is projected to grow by around 5.82%, while nominal growth is estimated at 8.89%.

Per-capita income is estimated at approximately ₹1.68 lakh.

The Economic Survey reports that over the preceding seven years, around 2,227 industrial units, involving investment of roughly ₹15,940 crore, became operational.

This reflects movement.

But investment announcements must not be confused with employment delivered.

A factory on a presentation slide does not provide a salary.

A memorandum of understanding is not an operational industry.

The next stage of transformation must therefore be judged by:

How many stable jobs are created?
How many local enterprises survive?
How much value is added to horticulture?
How many young people can build careers without leaving?
How many districts benefit beyond Srinagar and Jammu?

The old political economy survived by distributing government jobs, contracts and access through patronage.

The new economy must create opportunity beyond political recommendation.

Otherwise, development will remain visible in infrastructure but distant from households.

ENERGY: FROM POTENTIAL TO PRODUCTION

Major hydropower projects are now under construction, including:

— Pakal Dul: 1,000 MW
— Ratle: 850 MW
— Kiru: 624 MW
— Kwar: 540 MW

Together, these projects represent more than 3,000 MW of prospective generation capacity.

For a region with immense water resources but persistent power shortages, this is both opportunity and indictment.

Kashmir cannot indefinitely celebrate generation projects while households experience winter cuts.

The real success will come when hydropower is reflected not only in national capacity, but also in reliable local supply, fair benefits and visible economic returns.

THE MOST IMPORTANT TRANSFORMATION IS PSYCHOLOGICAL

The deepest change cannot be measured only in bridges, tourists or investment.

It lies in what Kashmir’s new generation now considers normal.
A generation once trained to recognize protest calendars is now discussing start-ups, examinations, sport, cinema, tourism, technology and entrepreneurship.
The romantic vocabulary of militancy has weakened.
The social prestige attached to street confrontation has declined.
Parents increasingly recognize that political entrepreneurs who glorified sacrifice rarely sacrificed their own children.

The separatist elite promised dignity through disorder.

But ordinary Kashmiris discovered that disorder always protects the powerful and punishes the poor.

The wealthy sent their children outside.

The shopkeeper remained behind a locked shutter.

The leader delivered speeches.

The labourer lost his wage.
The propagandist gained engagement.
The Kashmiri family received a funeral.
That business model has been disrupted.

BUT TRANSFORMATION IS NOT COMPLETION

A serious defence of 5 August must not become a denial of Kashmir’s unresolved problems.

Statehood remains pending.

Unemployment continues to frustrate young people.

Drug addiction has become a grave social emergency.

Power shortages remain unacceptable.

Recruitment processes require greater transparency.

Local businesses need protection against unequal competition.

Governance must become more accountable.

Terror networks continue to search for vulnerabilities.

And democratic institutions must be strengthened—not managed from a distance.

Peace cannot merely mean the absence of stones.

It must mean the presence of justice, opportunity, representation and responsive government.

Security created the space.

Politics and governance must now fill it.

SEVEN YEARS LATER

Before 2019, Kashmir was too often measured through:

=> Shutdown days.
=> Stone-pelting incidents.
=> Militant funerals.
=> Internet suspensions.
=> Boycott percentages.
=> Civilian casualties.
=> And economic losses.

Today, the conversation increasingly revolves around:

=> Voter turnout.
=> Tourist arrivals.
=> Rail connectivity.
=> Airport capacity.
=> Industrial units.
=> Investment.
=> Infrastructure.
=> And opportunity.

That is the transformation.

Not perfection.

Not the end of every conflict.

Not the disappearance of every grievance.

But a decisive change in direction.

5 August did not take Kashmir away from its identity.

It took away the monopoly of those who claimed that Kashmir’s identity could survive only through isolation, exceptionalism and endless instability.

Seven years later, the old ecosystem still mourns the loss of its political currency.

But Kashmir is no longer obliged to mourn with it.

The Valley has moved from enforced silence to democratic participation.

From shutdown calendars to train timetables.

From stone-pelting statistics to tourism figures.

From emotional exploitation to economic aspiration.

From a conflict managed by intermediaries to a future increasingly claimed by ordinary people.

5 August 2019 was not the day Kashmir lost its future.

It was the day those who had monopolized Kashmir’s future began losing control over it.

The transformation is visible.

The responsibility now is to deepen it, democratize it and ensure that its benefits reach every household.

Because the final measure of a new Kashmir will not be how loudly governments celebrate the change.

It will be how fully ordinary Kashmiris experience it.

DigiLocker is safer than a plastic folder — unless you download the fake app

On 29 November 2025, the official Digital India handle posted a warning that should have been louder than it was. Fraudulent apps with names like DigiLocker were circulating on app stores. The instruction was blunt: use only the authentic DigiLocker application. If you had already installed a suspicious version, delete it and change the passwords on linked accounts.

Moneycontrol reported the advisory the next day. Times of India followed for students. This is the incident. I am not going to invent a victim. The government warning is the case.

Why a plastic folder loses

A plastic folder can be stolen, soaked, or left on a bus. DigiLocker is safer than that folder for a simple reason. It is not a photo album of papers you scanned. It is a wallet that government issuers can push documents into.

The official site is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. From there you can access, share, and get government-issued documents verified: a driving licence, a vehicle RC, marksheets, and other records the issuer has actually placed in your account.

How it works, without the brochure language

You open an account that is authenticated with Aadhaar. Then an RTO, a school board, a university, or another issuer sends a digitally signed document into that account. When a verifier checks it, they are not squinting at a JPEG you uploaded. They are looking at the issuer's signature.

That is why a screenshot is not the same thing. A screenshot is a picture. An issued DigiLocker document is a signed record from the source. You can crop a marksheet photo in two minutes. You cannot forge the issuer's signature by taking a better photo.

MeitY has been clear on the legal point. Issued documents in DigiLocker are deemed at par with originals. The official about page says the same thing under the IT Act, and in more formal language under Rule 9A of the 2016 Digital Locker rules. You can show a digital driving licence, or pull a Class X or Class XII marksheet, without laminating another photocopy.

That legal status is useful only if you are inside the real locker.

The live warning

A clone that looks like DigiLocker does not need to "hack the government." It only needs you to type an Aadhaar number and share an OTP. DigiLocker does not make you unhackable. The risk moved. Paper used to get lost. Now someone tries to phish the OTP that opens the locker.

The authentic app is published by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Government of India. The official website is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. Install from there, or from the store listing that site points to. Confirm the developer name before you tap Install.

Do not install from a forwarded WhatsApp link. Do not trust a search ad that says "DigiLocker KYC" and asks for an OTP on a random page. No genuine officer needs that code from you on a link they just sent.

If a suspicious version is already on the phone, do what the advisory said. Delete it. Change the passwords on linked accounts. Then install the real app and check which documents are actually sitting there.

What to do before you need it

Before a road trip, open the real app and pull your driving licence and RC. Do it at home, on your own Wi-Fi, while you are not being rushed by a checkpoint or a rental desk.

Before admissions or a job file, students can pull marksheets from the board instead of hunting a laminated copy. If a verifier will accept DigiLocker, give them the issued document, not a crop of your screen.

Never share an OTP for "DigiLocker KYC" on a random link. The locker is tied to Aadhaar. The OTP is the key. Anyone who wants the key on a page you did not open from https://t.co/AE2sh860xw is not helping you file a document.

If you already downloaded something that only looked official, treat it as a live problem, not an embarrassing mistake. Delete the app. Change passwords. Watch bank and Aadhaar-linked SMS for a few days. Then start again from the official site.

The honest limit

A plastic folder fails when you lose it. DigiLocker fails when you hand the key to a lookalike. The folder is still worse for rain. The lookalike is worse for everything else.

Use the real locker. Pull the issued document, not a screenshot. Keep the OTP to yourself. That is the whole guide.

This article is written for general education and is not legal advice. It does not claim DigiLocker cannot be abused. The risk moved from lost paper to phishing for your Aadhaar OTP.

Sources: DigiLocker official site https://t.co/T2NXjM8lAm; DigiLocker About (issued documents at par with originals, IT Act / Rule 9A); MeitY statement that issued DigiLocker documents are deemed at par with originals; Digital India on X, 29 Nov 2025, authentic-app warning; Moneycontrol, 30 Nov 2025, fake DigiLocker apps advisory; Times of India Education, 11 Dec 2025, student guidance to use official sources.

We never planned to build a drone company.

But it still took 6 years of our lives.

Before starting the company, we spent 3 years just learning about UAVs. Studying, testing, failing, learning again.

In 2021, almost 95% of the drone parts we used were from China.

We did not like that at all.

So we said, "Let's build our own electronics in India."

We designed our own boards and sent them for fabrication.

That is when reality hit us.

Making the first samples in India was hard.
Turning them into mass production was even harder.

There were a lot of delays and quality issues.

Everyone had the necessary machines, but there was no clear way to know which factory could really do what.

Our first big dream failed fast.

So we changed direction.

We started building software to make imported drones fly on their own.

We worked on it for 8 months.

When it was finally ready, something big happened.

The Indian government banned the import of foreign drones.

Almost overnight, that software lost its target market.

We felt completely broken.

After that, we tried something even tougher.

We tried to build drones from scratch, with Indian made parts, in collaboration with other manufacturers.

Finding Indian suppliers felt like a treasure hunt.

Suppliers had all the machinery and infrastructure to build the components we needed.

But they did not know how to repurpose and use it better.

We ultimately couldn't succeed because of the harsh economics of electronics manufacturing in India.

In 2024, we shut down the drone company.

That was the end of the drone story.

But I kept one thing with me.

DigiLocker is safer than a plastic folder — unless you download the fake app

On 29 November 2025, the official Digital India handle posted a warning that should have been louder than it was. Fraudulent apps with names like DigiLocker were circulating on app stores. The instruction was blunt: use only the authentic DigiLocker application. If you had already installed a suspicious version, delete it and change the passwords on linked accounts.

Moneycontrol reported the advisory the next day. Times of India followed for students. This is the incident. I am not going to invent a victim. The government warning is the case.

Why a plastic folder loses

A plastic folder can be stolen, soaked, or left on a bus. DigiLocker is safer than that folder for a simple reason. It is not a photo album of papers you scanned. It is a wallet that government issuers can push documents into.

The official site is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. From there you can access, share, and get government-issued documents verified: a driving licence, a vehicle RC, marksheets, and other records the issuer has actually placed in your account.

How it works, without the brochure language

You open an account that is authenticated with Aadhaar. Then an RTO, a school board, a university, or another issuer sends a digitally signed document into that account. When a verifier checks it, they are not squinting at a JPEG you uploaded. They are looking at the issuer's signature.

That is why a screenshot is not the same thing. A screenshot is a picture. An issued DigiLocker document is a signed record from the source. You can crop a marksheet photo in two minutes. You cannot forge the issuer's signature by taking a better photo.

MeitY has been clear on the legal point. Issued documents in DigiLocker are deemed at par with originals. The official about page says the same thing under the IT Act, and in more formal language under Rule 9A of the 2016 Digital Locker rules. You can show a digital driving licence, or pull a Class X or Class XII marksheet, without laminating another photocopy.

That legal status is useful only if you are inside the real locker.

The live warning

A clone that looks like DigiLocker does not need to "hack the government." It only needs you to type an Aadhaar number and share an OTP. DigiLocker does not make you unhackable. The risk moved. Paper used to get lost. Now someone tries to phish the OTP that opens the locker.

The authentic app is published by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Government of India. The official website is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. Install from there, or from the store listing that site points to. Confirm the developer name before you tap Install.

Do not install from a forwarded WhatsApp link. Do not trust a search ad that says "DigiLocker KYC" and asks for an OTP on a random page. No genuine officer needs that code from you on a link they just sent.

If a suspicious version is already on the phone, do what the advisory said. Delete it. Change the passwords on linked accounts. Then install the real app and check which documents are actually sitting there.

What to do before you need it

Before a road trip, open the real app and pull your driving licence and RC. Do it at home, on your own Wi-Fi, while you are not being rushed by a checkpoint or a rental desk.

Before admissions or a job file, students can pull marksheets from the board instead of hunting a laminated copy. If a verifier will accept DigiLocker, give them the issued document, not a crop of your screen.

Never share an OTP for "DigiLocker KYC" on a random link. The locker is tied to Aadhaar. The OTP is the key. Anyone who wants the key on a page you did not open from https://t.co/AE2sh860xw is not helping you file a document.

If you already downloaded something that only looked official, treat it as a live problem, not an embarrassing mistake. Delete the app. Change passwords. Watch bank and Aadhaar-linked SMS for a few days. Then start again from the official site.

The honest limit

A plastic folder fails when you lose it. DigiLocker fails when you hand the key to a lookalike. The folder is still worse for rain. The lookalike is worse for everything else.

Use the real locker. Pull the issued document, not a screenshot. Keep the OTP to yourself. That is the whole guide.

This article is written for general education and is not legal advice. It does not claim DigiLocker cannot be abused. The risk moved from lost paper to phishing for your Aadhaar OTP.

A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

These are separate from blocking directions issued under Section 69A of the IT Act.

The report also says Meta has integrated its API with Sahyog to comply with the government’s 2–3-hour deadline, potentially allowing content flagged through government directions to be blocked automatically without a separate human review.

Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

You know what's normal? Corruption and mismanagement. So many countries around the world are led by governments, frequently authoritarian, which have persistently mismanaged their economies. 

Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Turkey, India etc. are all performing far below their potential because of policy failures connected to corruption and elite politics.

Notwithstanding its own corruption and mismanagement, Iran was actually outperforming many of these countries in delivering economic welfare until 2012. Ordinary Iranians were getting consistently richer until the sanctions really tightened that year.

What makes Iran unique *is* the sanctions. It is their pervasive and extreme impact that distinguishes Iran from other "normally mismanaged" countries. Unlike every other country experiencing economic malaise around the world, neither the Iranian state nor the private sector can engage in routine commerce. Iran cannot freely export its oil and non-oil goods and it even struggles to efficiently import food. The country faces a persistent and wholly artificial balance of payments crisis because of expansive U.S. sanctions pushed by your employer.

Who's to blame for this situation? You want to blame Iran's leaders for this predicament. In your view, it's their fault that they have undertaken policies that led them to be sanctioned by Trump. Assigning blame solely on one side is obviously ahistorical and reductive, but for the sake of argument let's say its correct and that only Iran should be blamed for the imposition of the sanctions. Does that actually absolve the U.S. from responsibility for the pain faced by ordinary Iranians? Absolutely not, because they U.S. is not just causing the hardship, it is also denying ordinary Iranians the means to alleviate the economic pain they are enduring.

Once again, we can look to other countries for a guide. When an economic crisis hits Pakistan or Argentina or South Africa, ordinary people take matters into their own hands. When things get really extreme, one form of recourse is emigration. Those who do emigrate send remittances back to their countries to support their suffering family members. Ordinary Iranians cannot do this. They are uniquely encumbered by U.S. sanctions and related policies.

If they can get a visa, Iranians can scarcely afford to emigrate to most countries and are banned from the U.S. altogether by racist policies. Those who are abroad cannot easily send money back to Iran because U.S. sanctions policy makes banks and money service businesses cower from processing payments to Iranian bank accounts.

So in effect, the sanctions have created a crisis, trapped ordinary Iranians in the crisis, and denied them the means to shield themselves from the pain of the crisis. Even if you refuse to believe that "maximum pressure" sanctions are an abnormal and amoral tool or that the U.S. government should be held responsible for their imposition, you cannot skirt the fact that sanctions deny Iranians the basic means to protect themselves from the fallout of sanctions ostensibly intended to target elites. People are getting poorer, hungrier, more desperate in a country that until quite recently had a large and growing middle class.

These conditions arose because the goal of sanctions stopped being "behavior change" years ago. The goal is to turn Iran into a weak and dysfunctional state, even if that means crushing the livelihoods and aspirations of 90 million people.

The Trump administration keeps speaking of the Islamic Republic as a "sinking ship." If ordinary people were a priority, they'd at least be thrown a lifeline. But in Iran, as in Cuba, Afghanistan, and Venezuela, people are being left to drown and people like you, who hold the rope in their hands, stand there blaming the Iranian regime for your own lack of moral action.

This framing is either intellectually lazy or purposefully crafted to mislead, and it abandons the first duty of serious analysis: locating causation where the evidence puts it.

Every government's baseline responsibility is to pursue foreign and economic policies that serve its people's prosperity. Tehran has done the opposite for three decades and the record predates U.S. secondary sanctions by a wide margin. 

The Majles Research Center itself documented in 1999 that 63.5% of privatizations between 1989 and 1998 went to foundations and parastatals, not a real private sector, not to the ordinary Iranians. Khamenei's Article 44 decree transferring the commanding heights to IRGC-linked and bonyad entities was issued in May 2005, five years before CISADA was passed in the U.S. Congress. That is what I'd call khosulati capture, not U.S. sanctions.

U.S. messaging has often been poor and, yes, that critique is fair. But sanctions are imposed in response to national security threats: nuclear escalation, ballistic missile proliferation, terrorism financing, hostage-taking. What Washington and the international community ask of Tehran; stop enriching to weapons-grade, stop arming proxies, stop killing dissidents abroad; are reasonable expectations of any responsible state.

Iranians are impoverished by their own regime's choices. Pretending otherwise isn't analysis but merely advocacy presented as analysis.

The FTC gets authority over age verification standards, content safety audits, data broker registries, social media research, chatbot rules, gaming platform safety, educational resources, advertising regulations, and enforcement of the entire act. The FTC becomes the operational regulator of the American internet. This is the largest federal power grab over online platforms in a decade, buried inside a children's safety bill where nobody will vote against it.

⚠️⚠️3. It forces companies to spy on children to prove they are protecting them.**

The audit requirements mandate platforms track and report how many minors use their service, how long they spend, what safety features they use, what reports they file, and what personal information is collected. The data broker rules exempt Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft because their product is advertising services, not data sales. Your coding agent's compliance score looks good because it counts rules the model follows without you asking.

A team at ByteDance Seed built Harness-IF to prove it. The benchmark scores coding agents on 256 individual rules across 60 real multi-turn coding tasks, and it comes with a new metric that exposes the inflation.

They call it AP-Acc. Standard benchmarks count every rule an agent follows. AP-Acc strips out the rules the model was going to follow anyway and scores only the ones that require it to change its behavior.

To figure out which rules are freebies, they ran the same tasks after removing the target rule. If models follow the rule on their own, that rule doesn't test obedience. AP-Acc scores only the rest.

Across 12 frontier models, every single one scored worse on rules that pushed against default behavior. The gap ranged from 3.6 to 7.4 points. Aggregate compliance scores overstate how obedient your agent is, and the inflation varies by model, so you can't subtract a constant to correct for it.

Claude Opus 4.7 topped every column. But it dropped 7.3 points on rules it wouldn't have followed on its own.

The paper surfaces two more findings.

Where you place the instruction matters. System prompts, project files, and direct user messages all tied for highest precedence in conflict tests. Tool descriptions and skill descriptions ranked lower. The assumption that later instructions win doesn't hold.

And 77% of agent failures are omissions, not overreach. The agent didn't do what you told it to. It didn't go rogue. It forgot. Omission is harder to catch because the output looks fine. What's missing is what breaks things.

Output control rules hit the lowest accuracy for 11 of the 12 models. No model cleared 79% on them.

If you build on top of coding agents and trust them to follow your operational rules, the compliance number on the leaderboard isn't telling you what you think it is.

I run compliance at Deutsche Bank.

My job is to make sure we follow the rules.

I'm very good at my job.

In 2013, a junior analyst flagged a series of transactions.

The transactions were unusual.

The client was unusual.

The client was Jeffrey Epstein.

The analyst wrote a report.

The report was thorough.

It named the client.

It named the transactions.

It named the pattern.

I read the report.

I flagged it.

Not the transactions.

The analyst.

She was "not a cultural fit."

That's not a banking term.

It's an HR term.

HR is where compliance sends its problems.

The transactions continued.

The analyst did not.

For six years, the account remained open.

I signed off on it quarterly.

Quarterly review means I looked at the numbers.

The numbers were large.

Large numbers are good for the bank.

Good numbers don't get flagged.

That's the system.

In 2019, the client was arrested.

I learned this from the news.

Not from our compliance system.

Our compliance system doesn't flag arrests.

It flags analysts.

The client died in custody.

That simplified things.

Dead clients don't generate new transactions.

Existing transactions were already approved.

By me.

In 2023, we paid $75 million.

That sounds like a lot.

It is not a lot.

We made more than that from the account.

The settlement included no admission of wrongdoing.

We admitted nothing.

That is what $75 million buys.

Not innocence.

Silence.

The analyst who flagged the account in 2013 was not part of the settlement.

She was not rehired.

She was not compensated.

She was not mentioned.

She was right in 2013.

She is still unemployed in 2026.

I am still employed.

I was promoted in 2021.

The promotion was for "excellence in risk management."

I managed the risk.

The risk was the analyst.

Now the files are public.

People are reading names.

They are reading transaction records.

They are reading the report the analyst wrote in 2013.

The report I flagged.

The report that got her fired.

It says everything.

It said everything then.

Nobody read it.

I read it.

I flagged the analyst.

The transactions continued.

The analyst did not.

That is compliance.

I have a plaque on my desk.

It says "Integrity First."

It came with the promotion.

Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

“Cockroach Janta Party Protest”
The Dehumanization and Subversion Project

Details of the process of how a republic is dismantled long before anyone tries to overthrow it. Decoding the disturbing trend of vile abuse of elected leaders and law enforcement, and also the open call to dismantle the Indian Constitution as a righteous form of protest.

In Delhi, over these past few days, men in a crowd bent down, picked up stones that had been deliberately placed there for them, and hurled those stones at police and law enforcement personnel who were doing their duty. Somewhere in that same crowd, personnel of the Delhi Police and the Rapid Action Force were surrounded, dragged, beaten, and left fighting for their lives.

Vehicles were torched. Public property was smashed. Private property was destroyed. Streets that exist to carry citizens were converted into battlegrounds. Institutions that exist to protect civil order were converted into targets.

From the same ecosystem that describes itself as peaceful, from the same platforms that speak endlessly about rights, democracy, conscience, dissent, and constitutional morality, came open threats against a sitting Prime Minister, a sitting Home Minister, a sitting Education Minister, and against the men and women who wear the uniform of the Indian Army.

Hold that image steady. Do not look away from it.

The vocabulary of protest should not be allowed to blur the reality of violence. Slogans should not be allowed to deodorize savagery. The word "student" should not be allowed to erase the act of picking up a stone and aiming it at another human being's skull.

This essay argues that what we are watching has two architectures rather than one. The first is moral, and it operates inside the mind. It lowers the cost of harming a human being by first reducing that human being to a symbol. The second is operational, and it operates in the street, the courtroom, the newsroom, and the donor network. It is written down, it is taught, and it has been applied in country after country with a consistency that no honest observer can call coincidental.

The two architectures require each other. The manual cannot work until the moral preparation is complete, because ordinary young people will not attack a police officer they still see as a person. The moral preparation accomplishes nothing on its own until an organization arrives to convert it into a schedule of actions. Understand them separately, and you will misread the event. Understand them together and the whole thing becomes legible.

Begin with the question that India's self-appointed conscience keepers desperately do not want asked.

When a person crosses from dissent into violence, from protest into intimidation, from disagreement into threats of murder, does that person still get to hide behind the sanctity of ordinary civic protest?

What India Has to Recognize
The issue is far larger than one protest. It is the repeated normalization of a method, and the method now has a stated objective spoken aloud on a national broadcaster.

The goal is delegitimization rather than debate. The goal is to make governance impossible unless the elected government submits to unelected street pressure. The goal is to teach the public that certain ideological groups possess a permanent right to disrupt national life whenever democracy disappoints them. Above all, the goal is to move the moral Overton Window far enough that abuse becomes normal, threats become acceptable, and violence becomes negotiable.

This is why none of it can be treated as an accident.

Stones do not place themselves on streets. Mobs do not spontaneously discover identical slogans. Young people do not accidentally arrive at the same vocabulary of contempt. Political ecosystems do not coincidentally produce the same moral script across campuses, media platforms, activist networks, and street confrontations. Movements separated by continents and decades do not independently reinvent the same five-step ladder.

This is cultivated. This is rehearsed. This is funded. This is rewarded. This is protected by narrative managers who arrive after the violence to explain why the violent are actually the wounded conscience of the nation.

A nation that wants to survive has to refuse the lie.

The police officer bleeding on the street is a person and not an abstraction. So is the soldier being threatened. So is the elected leader being abused. So is the voter whose mandate is being delegitimized. So is the shopkeeper whose property is burned. So is the citizen trapped behind a blockade. So, for that matter, is the nineteen-year-old who genuinely came to Jantar Mantar because he believed an examination had been rigged and who has no idea he is being driven up somebody else's ladder.

Their rights matter too. Their dignity matters too. Their safety matters too. Their democracy matters too. A republic cannot allow one class of political actor to monopolize victimhood while imposing the costs on everyone else.

So let us state the principle clearly.

If you want to oppose the government, then oppose it.

Write. Speak. Organize. Campaign. File petitions. Contest elections. Persuade citizens. Win votes.

That is democracy, and India offers more room for it than almost any society at its income level in history.

If you pick up stones, if you burn vehicles, if you assault police officers, if you issue death threats, if you turn public streets into theaters of intimidation, if you announce on air that Parliament has been superseded by the crowd, then you are attacking democracy rather than practicing it. When society says so plainly, that is civilization defending its minimum conditions, and it is a long way from authoritarianism.

The real test of a democracy lies beyond whether it permits dissent.

AN OPEN LETTER TO THE WNBA
Ambiguity invites absurdity.
Last week yours produced two grown men declaring for the WNBA draft. One of them is six-foot-ten.
I have spent close to forty years reading documents other people wrote. Contracts, statutes, plea agreements, ordinances nobody has opened since Nixon. The most dangerous sentence in any of them is not the one that says something wrong. It is the one that sounds finished and isn't.
I will confess something before I say a word about yours. I have left language soft on purpose. Most lawyers have. You leave a word loose because pinning it down means having the fight today, in the room, with people who are tired and want to go home. So you let it ride. You tell yourself everybody in here knows what that means. Then years later somebody who was never in that room reads it cold, and it turns out nobody knew, and it is not your call anymore.
You have a new collective bargaining agreement this season. The eligibility section says only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA.
Now look for the definition.
There isn't one. No test, no standard, no sentence anywhere saying what the word means. Reporters went looking this month for a policy explaining how transgender or intersex eligibility actually gets decided in your league. They could not find one, and when they asked you, nobody answered.
The value, though, you have broadcast for a decade. On August 1 one of your coaches told reporters that every kid has a right to sports, and she has worn the shirts and written the op-eds to match. Your players union released a statement embracing justice, equity, diversity and inclusion. Nobody has to guess where you stand. You have told us at volume for years.
So two former NBA players read your rulebook, took your stated value at its word, and applied it to themselves.
Your commissioner sent teams a memo calling the matter complex and nuanced, said fair competition remains a high priority, and handed it to a task force of team presidents and general managers meeting this week. Your union said its players will not be used as political pawns.
Watch what did not happen there.
Nobody answered with the rule. There was no rule to answer with.
You cannot enforce a definition you were too afraid to write.
What came back instead was an argument about motive. You are saying these men do not really mean it, and maybe they don't. But a standard that only holds when the institution approves of your reasons is not a standard. It is a mood.
Let me be fair to you, because you have a point that deserves saying out loud instead of shouted past.
No player born male has ever played in your league as an openly transgender woman. Not one, ever. Anybody selling a five-alarm fire at the professional level is selling something. And that same coach said something in the same breath that almost nobody quoted, which is that this question needs real nuance once you get past puberty into elite competition, and that reasonable people ought to be able to find common ground.
She is right about puberty, and that concession is the entire argument, which is worth sitting with for a second because she is the one who made it and nobody made her.
Male puberty builds a longer skeleton, a bigger heart and lungs, denser bone, more fast-twitch fiber, a wider hand. No announcement reverses any of it. Women's sports exist as a separate category for that reason and no other.
What a grown adult does privately with their own body is between them, their doctor and their God. It is a different question entirely from who lines up across from a nineteen-year-old with a scholarship on the line.
If you raised a daughter, coached one, or sat in the bleachers while one learned what it meant to compete, you already know the difference.
And let me be unfair to my own side.
Those two men did not fix anything last week. They made content. One of them lasted three games in the NBA more than a decade ago. The other had an eleven-year NBA career. They will both get a week of bookings, a spike in downloads and a merch cycle out of this, and then they will move on, because that is the business they are in now. The problem does not move on. It stays exactly where it was, on somebody else's desk, and that somebody does not have a podcast.
A stunt is not a standard. It only proves one is missing.
Tennis has already been through all of this, and it is worth two minutes of your time.
In 2013 Serena Williams said men's and women's tennis were almost two different sports, and that Andy Murray would beat her 6-0, 6-0. The room laughed with her. Four years later John McEnroe said essentially the same thing and was a misogynist by lunch.
But the woman who matters most to this argument is not Serena Williams.
It is Martina Navratilova, who has spent seven years saying it and taking the beating for it. Martina and I have tangled before, and we agree on very little. She endorsed Kamala Harris. She has never had a kind word for this president. She came out in the 1980s when it cost something real. Her old coach, Renée Richards, was one of the first professional athletes in this country to transition publicly, and she coached Martina to two Wimbledon titles. She still says women's sports are not a place for failed male athletes.
When somebody I argue with that often lands where I land, I listen harder, not less.
Billie Jean King, who built the same house with her, disagrees. King has signed the briefs and given the interviews and says inclusion is the point.
Two women. Same generation, same fight, same trophy case. They cannot agree.
That is precisely why you write it down. When the two people who built the category land in opposite places, that is not a reason to stay quiet. That is a siren telling you somebody has to decide and put a name on it.
And here is what makes your silence so strange. Nearly everybody else already found the nerve to pick a side.
Twenty-seven states passed laws. The NCAA rewrote its policy and limited women's competition to athletes assigned female at birth. The United States Olympic and Paralympic Committee, a separate body from the IOC, did the same. The WTA adopted an eligibility policy built around screening for the SRY gene, ordinarily by saliva, cheek swab or blood, and is catching real fire for it from doctors who call the test too blunt and privacy advocates who have a point.
They do not all use the same rule. They do not even all agree on the science. But at least you can find the rule.
And on June 30 the Supreme Court held that Title IX permits schools to limit girls' and women's teams to biological females, and that the Idaho and West Virginia laws do not violate equal protection. Justice Kavanaugh framed the question as whether schools may determine eligibility for women's and girls' sports based on biological sex, and answered that they may.
Read that last word carefully. May.
The Court did not order anybody to do anything. It handed the decision back to the institutions and told them it is theirs to make. Which means you have now been handed this question twice, once by the country and once by the Court, and your answer both times has been a meeting.
Every one of those bodies took incoming for deciding. That is what happens when you write something down. A written rule has an author. It can be argued with, appealed, amended, repealed. Somebody stands behind it in daylight and eats the criticism.
A blank page cannot be appealed. It can only be walked through.
Now here is the part almost nobody talks about, and it is the question nobody asks.
Where are the laws protecting the boys?
Go read those state statutes instead of the headlines about them. In Florida, in West Virginia and in others, the legislature answered both halves in the same breath. Girls may play on boys' teams. Boys may not play on girls' teams.
One paragraph. Two directions. Only one of them needed a rule.
The Court did it too. There is a footnote in that opinion saying nothing in it should be read to limit biological females competing on male or co-ed teams.
Nobody marched about that half. No task force was convened to protect the boys. Nobody built a movement to keep the girls out.
And sure, it happens. A girl makes varsity as a placekicker and it is national news for a week. A girl keeps goal on the boys' side and holds her own. Good for her, seriously. But notice where it happens, which is the handful of spots where the physical gap matters least, and notice that when it does happen nobody files anything. Nobody has ever needed to.
Everybody already knows why. That is the thing nobody will say into a microphone, and it is the only reason any of this is treated as difficult.
So decide. If self-identification is your standard, then those two men qualify and you should stand up and say so out loud. If biology is your standard, publish it and defend it like everybody else has had to.
You do not get to hold both and pick between them based on who is asking.
And understand what is actually on the table while you deliberate.
You spent twenty-nine years being told this would not last. Now attendance is up thirty-four percent to over three million. Your national viewership is the best it has been since 1998, and you outdrew the NHL. Your All-Star game pulled 3.2 million this July, up forty-four percent in a year. And you are one season into an eleven-year media deal that grew from two point two billion dollars to three point one.
You are still arguing with your own players about whether any of it counts as profit yet. Which means every bit of that is a bet on people who just showed up and have not committed to anything yet.
That is the moment you have chosen to be undecided in, with the ink barely dry on the deal.
You finally got America to look. This is a hell of a time to blink.
Keep stalling and this stops being a policy question. It becomes a bit. Every former player with a phone and a grievance gets a free week of attention at your expense, and your players spend their season answering questions about it instead of playing. You will be a circus, and not the good kind, and not one of the women who built this will have done anything to earn that.
I have watched a lot of your games this season. Your officials have not been shy. Quick whistle, quick technical, and the message is always the same. Somebody has to make the call, and it will not be the crowd.
Take your own advice. Because if you will not make this call, it gets made anyway, just not by you.
None of us out here are wearing stripes. We do not need to be. There is no review on the call the crowd makes. No appeal, and nobody at the table to hear your side.
It just shows up as an empty seat.
Which brings me to the people whose opinion on this outranks yours and mine both.
The women.
If you are a woman reading this, this part belongs to you.
You built this. Equal prize money at the Open did not fall out of the sky in 1973, somebody stood in a room and demanded it. And nobody handed this league those three million seats. Women filled them. That was work, generations of it, and it is worth one written sentence.
Men should not compete in women's sports.
Not in the WNBA. Not on a college roster. Not in a Pasco County gym on a Friday night, floor wax and a buzzer and somebody's grandmother three rows up in a folding chair she brought from home.
But here is what actually keeps me up, and it is true whether you agree with that last line or not.
I am not really writing to a league. You have lawyers, a commissioner, a communications department and a task force. You will survive this either way, and you know it.
The person who cannot is an athletic director in some small district, in an office that smells like copier toner, with a schedule magnet on the filing cabinet from a printing company that went under years ago. A mother sits down across from him and asks a simple question about who her fifteen-year-old is competing against on Friday. He has no task force. No general counsel down the hall, nobody drafting a memo. He has a binder with nothing in the relevant tab, and he has to answer her before the bus leaves Thursday.
Your ambiguity becomes his responsibility.
A league can convene committees until the leaves turn. That man cannot.
So whether you agree with me or think I am dead wrong, do me one favor this week.
Find out what rule your granddaughter is actually playing under.
Pull up your own school district's policy. Not the mission statement. Not the values page. The actual policy. Find the sentence.
Then see whether there is a second one.
